items.title: The Ready Position
items.objective: The player will be able to get into a balanced ready position before every pitch, with feet wider than the shoulders, knees bent, and hands out in front.
items.summary: Every fielding play starts before the ball is hit. This lesson teaches the athletic ready position young fielders should be in as the pitch crosses the plate.

video.note: The production video will show a 6-year-old and a 10-year-old side by side moving from standing upright into the ready position on the coach's call, with a freeze frame marking the feet, knees, bottom, and hands.

explanation: A fielder cannot react to a ball if the body is standing straight up. The ready position is the way baseball players stand before every pitch so they can move in any direction the moment the ball is hit. Think of a goalkeeper waiting for a penalty kick or a tennis player waiting for a serve. The body is low, loose, and leaning slightly forward.

Start with the feet. They should be wider than the shoulders, with the toes pointing a little bit out and the weight on the balls of the feet, not the heels. A good check is to ask the child to wiggle their toes; if they can feel their toes pressing into their shoes, the weight is in the right place.

Next, bend the knees and push the bottom down and back, like starting to sit in a chair that is a little too far away. The back stays fairly flat and the chest stays up so the eyes can see the batter. The child should feel the muscles in the front of their legs working a little.

Finally, the hands. Both hands come out in front of the body, around knee height, with the glove open and facing the batter. Hands resting on the knees look comfortable, but they are stuck there; hands floating in front of the body can drop straight to the ground for a grounder or lift for a pop-up.

Older beginners add a tiny hop called a pre-pitch step. As the pitcher releases the ball, the fielder takes a small hop and lands in the ready position, so the legs are already loaded like springs when the bat meets the ball. For ages 4-6 the hop is optional; standing still in a good ready position is the whole goal.
parentInstructions: You do not need a ball for this lesson. Stand 10 feet in front of your child and pretend to be the batter.
Say 'Pitcher's ready!' and have your child drop into the ready position. Count to three while they hold it, then say 'Relax!'
Walk around and check four things in order: feet wider than shoulders, knees bent, bottom down, hands out in front and not on the knees.
Fix only one thing per repetition. If the feet and the hands are both wrong, fix the feet first and ignore the hands until the feet are right three times in a row.
Ask your child to show you how a kid who is NOT ready stands (straight up, hands at sides), then show you ready. The contrast helps them feel the difference.
Keep the whole thing under five minutes and finish with a silly freeze so it ends in laughter.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: This lesson needs no equipment at all. A chalk home plate or a doormat gives the child a batter to face.
steps: Stand up tall facing the parent, who plays the batter.
On 'Pitcher's ready!' step the feet out wider than the shoulders and point the toes slightly out.
Bend the knees and push the bottom down and back until the thighs feel like they are working.
Bring both hands out in front of the body at knee height, glove open toward the batter.
Hold still and count to three with the eyes on the batter the whole time.
On 'Relax!' stand up, shake out the legs, and get ready for the next call.
After five good freezes, add a tiny two-foot hop that lands in the ready position on the call.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands resting on the knees.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child hold a pretend tray of cookies in front of the body; the tray cannot touch the knees.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing straight-legged with the bottom high in the air.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask them to pretend to sit on a stool that is just behind them, then stop halfway down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Weight back on the heels, so the child rocks backward.
commonMistakes.fix: Say 'wiggle your toes' and have them lean until they feel the toes press into the shoe.

commonMistakes.mistake: Feet together or only shoulder width apart.
commonMistakes.fix: Put two pieces of tape or two leaves on the ground wider than their shoulders and have them land on the marks.

safety: Practice on dry, flat ground; a hopping child can slip on a wet garage floor or a loose rug.
Keep siblings and pets out of the hopping zone so nobody gets stepped on.
Short sessions only. Holding a squat is tiring for small legs, so five freezes with rest beats twenty in a row.

progression.easier: Skip the hop and let the child hold the position for only one second, then build to three.
progression.harder: Add the pre-pitch hop, then have the child react to a point: parent points left, right, or down and the child takes one quick step that way from the ready position.

items.title: The Fielding Triangle: Feet Wide, Glove Out Front
items.objective: The player will be able to field a rolled or slow ground ball in the fielding triangle, with the feet wide, the glove out in front of the body, and the ball watched all the way into the glove.
items.summary: The fielding triangle is the shape a good infielder makes with two feet and the glove. Learn it here and every ground ball lesson that follows will make sense.

video.note: The production video will show an overhead camera angle of a 9-year-old fielding rolled ground balls, with a triangle drawn on screen connecting the two feet and the glove, plus a slow-motion close-up of the bare hand closing over the ball.

explanation: Picture a triangle on the ground. Two corners are the fielder's feet, spread wider than the shoulders. The third corner, the point of the triangle, is the glove, reaching out in front of the body. That shape is what coaches mean when they say 'get in the triangle,' and it is the single most important idea in fielding ground balls.

The glove belongs at the point of the triangle for a simple reason: the eyes can see it there. When the glove is tucked back between the feet, the child has to look almost straight down and loses the ball in the last foot of its travel. When the glove is out front, the child can see the ball and the glove in the same picture and watch the ball roll in.

Get low to make the triangle. The knees bend, the bottom drops toward the ground, and the back stays flat enough that a cup of water would sit on it. The glove opens with the fingers pointing at the ground and the palm facing the ball, and the bare hand hovers just above the glove like the top jaw of an alligator.

As the ball arrives, the eyes stay on it until it disappears into the pocket. The bare hand closes over the top so the ball cannot bounce out, and then both hands pull back toward the belly button. Coaches call that pulling motion the funnel; it will become the start of the throw in later lessons.

Right-handed throwers set up with the left foot a few inches ahead of the right, which puts the body in position to start the throwing footwork. Left-handed throwers mirror that with the right foot slightly ahead. At this stage, though, a wide, low, balanced triangle matters far more than which foot is forward.
parentInstructions: Kneel or crouch 12 to 15 feet from your child. Being low makes your rolls straighter and lets you see the child's glove.

Roll underhand with a bowling motion: step with the opposite foot, swing the arm back, and release the ball low so it rolls instead of bouncing. Aim at the glove, which for a right-handed child is on their left side.
Start every roll slow and straight. Only roll a little to one side after five clean catches in a row.
Before each roll, wait until you can see the triangle: two feet wide and the glove reaching toward you with fingers pointing down.
Watch the head as the ball arrives. If it lifts to look at you, say 'eyes in the glove' and roll the next one even slower.
Use a tennis ball or a soft safety ball on a driveway. Never roll a hard baseball on concrete, where it skips unpredictably.
Ten minutes is plenty. End on a catch, not a miss.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a sock ball across the living room carpet and field it with bare hands. The triangle, the low body, and the eyes on the ball are identical.
steps: Child starts in the ready position; parent kneels 12 to 15 feet away with a tennis ball.
Parent calls 'triangle' and the child drops low: feet wider than shoulders, bottom down, glove reaching out front with fingers pointing at the ground.
Parent rolls the ball slowly straight at the glove.
Child watches the ball roll into the glove and closes the bare hand over the top like an alligator mouth.
Child pulls both hands to the belly button and holds the ball up to show the parent.
Child rolls or flips the ball back underhand and resets in the ready position.
After eight rolls, parent freezes the child at the moment of the catch and checks glove out front, bottom down, head still.
Finish with five rolls one step to the glove side so the child learns to move the feet first, then make the triangle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove tucked between the feet or under the body.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a chalk mark or a leaf on the ground a foot in front of the toes and ask the child to touch it with the glove before each roll.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing tall and bending only at the waist.
commonMistakes.fix: Say 'bottom down' and have the child touch the ground with the back of the glove before the ball comes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Head lifts to look at the parent before the ball is caught.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask the child to tell you what color the ball is as it enters the glove; they cannot answer without looking.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bare hand hangs at the side, so the ball pops out.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice the alligator chomp with no ball, then roll three balls where the only job is to cover the ball with the bare hand.

safety: Tennis balls or soft safety balls only for driveway and garage work; a hard baseball skips off concrete into faces.
Clear the rolling lane of bikes, toys, and cars, and face the child away from the street.
Check the grass for holes and sticks before rolling in a yard or park.

progression.easier: Roll a sock ball from 8 feet and let the child field with bare hands, bucket-style, until the low body position feels normal.
progression.harder: Roll firmer balls from 20 feet, alternate glove side and bare-hand side, and ask for the right-left footwork after the funnel.

items.title: Rolled Ground Balls: First Fielding Steps
items.objective: The player will be able to stop a slowly rolled soft ball with two hands, pick it up, and hold it against the belly.
items.summary: A four-year-old's first ground ball should be a slow roll into two open hands. This lesson gives parents a gentle, step-by-step way to teach the very first fielding skills.

video.note: The production video will show a parent sitting on a living room floor rolling a sock ball to a 4-year-old using bucket hands, then the same child a few weeks later fielding a soft safety ball in a backyard with a small glove.

explanation: At ages 4 to 6, fielding is really about three things: watching a moving object, getting the body in front of it, and using two hands. A glove is optional at the start and often gets in the way, because a stiff new glove is hard for small hands to close. Bare hands teach the right habits faster.

Teach bucket hands first. The child holds both hands out in front, palms up, pinkies touching, fingers pointing toward the ground. The hands look like a bucket or a scoop. A rolling ball goes straight into the bucket, and the child lifts it to the belly and hugs it.

The body position is a small version of what older kids do. Feet apart, knees bent, bottom down low, and the bucket out in front where the child can see it. Tiny children get low easily; the challenge is keeping them from sitting all the way down on the ground.

Rolls should be slow enough that the child can watch the whole trip from the parent's hand to the bucket. Say 'ball!' as it leaves the hand so the child's eyes find it early. Most misses at this age come from looking at the parent's face instead of the ball, which is why the parent should sit low and quiet.

Moving to the ball comes next. Roll one a single step to the side and let the child slide the feet to get in front of it, then make the bucket. Feet first, then hands is a rule that will follow the child all the way to the big field.
parentInstructions: Sit or kneel on the floor 6 to 8 feet from your child. Being at their eye level makes you less distracting and your rolls gentler.
Show bucket hands with your own hands first and have the child copy you. Say the words 'bucket hands' every time until they say it back.
Roll underhand along the ground, slowly, straight at the bucket. Say 'ball!' as you release so their eyes go to it.
Celebrate the catch by having them hold the ball up and show you; that habit of hugging the ball to the belly and then showing it becomes the funnel later.
Do not correct how they roll the ball back. One skill at a time.
Stop after 15 to 20 rolls, or sooner if attention drifts. Ending early keeps them asking to play again.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A rolled-up pair of socks on a carpet or a smooth floor is the ideal first ball. It cannot hurt, it rolls slowly, and the child can field it with bare hands.
steps: Sit on the floor facing the child, 6 to 8 feet apart.
Both of you make bucket hands: palms up, pinkies together, fingers pointing down.
Child spreads the feet, bends the knees, and holds the bucket out front, low to the ground.
Parent says 'ball!' and rolls the sock ball slowly along the ground into the bucket.
Child scoops the ball with both hands and hugs it to the belly.
Child holds the ball up high to show the parent, then rolls it back.
After ten scoops in a row, parent rolls one a single step to the left and the next a single step to the right.
Finish with three easy rolls straight to the bucket so the session ends with success.

commonMistakes.mistake: Child looks at the parent instead of the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Sit lower and go quiet; ask them to call out the color of the ball as it reaches their hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands come together late, after the ball has already passed through.
commonMistakes.fix: Have them make the bucket before you roll and hold it there; say 'bucket first, then ball.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Child sits down on the ground to field.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a sticker on each knee and tell them the stickers must not touch the floor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Child runs toward the roller and grabs the ball out of the air.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a shoe between you as a line they must stay behind until the ball crosses it.

safety: Sock balls and soft safety balls only; a child this age should never field a hard baseball.
Choose a spot away from coffee tables, stairs, and anything with corners, because the child will chase a ball that gets past.
If a glove is used, make sure it is small, soft, and already broken in so the child can close it.

progression.easier: Roll from 4 feet while the child sits on the floor with legs apart, so the ball cannot get by and every roll is a catch.
progression.harder: Stand up and roll from 10 feet with a soft safety ball, add a glove with the bare hand covering, and roll two steps to each side.

items.title: Glove Positioning: Fingers Down, Fingers Up
items.objective: The player will be able to turn the glove fingers-down for balls below the waist and fingers-up for balls above the waist without being told which is coming.
items.summary: Most dropped balls at this age come from a glove pointed the wrong way. This lesson teaches the one rule that fixes it: below the belt, fingers down; above the belt, fingers up.

video.note: The production video will show close-ups of a child's glove turning from fingers-down to fingers-up as the toss height changes, with a horizontal line drawn at belt height on screen and a slow-motion example of a ball rolling under a fingers-up glove.

explanation: A glove is just a big hand, and like a hand it can only catch a ball if the open side faces where the ball is coming from. The rule that young players need is short enough to remember on the field. For a ball that will arrive below the belt, the fingers of the glove point down at the ground. For a ball that will arrive above the belt, the fingers point up at the sky.

Fingers down means the glove hangs from the wrist like a scoop, with the palm facing the ball and the pinky side near the ground. In this position a low ball or a grounder rolls up into the pocket. If a child keeps the fingers up on a low ball, the ball hits the heel of the glove or slips underneath it, which is the most common miss in tee ball.

Fingers up means the glove sits in front of the chest or face with the thumb side toward the middle of the body and the pocket open to the ball. The bare hand comes alongside to trap the ball once it arrives. Many kids try to catch chest-high balls with the glove upside down and the palm facing the ground, so the ball bounces off the back of the glove.

The belt line is the switch. Teach the child to look at where the ball is going to arrive, not where it is right now, and decide down or up before it gets there. In the beginning the parent calls it out; within a couple of sessions most children call it themselves and then stop needing to say it at all.

Keep the glove relaxed. A squeezed, stiff glove cannot open wide, and a child who snaps the glove shut before the ball arrives will knock it away. Say 'soft hands' and let the ball close the glove instead of the child closing it early.
parentInstructions: Stand 8 feet from your child with a soft safety ball. Closer is better for this lesson because you are teaching a position, not a reaction.
Call 'Down!' and toss a gentle underhand ball that arrives at the knees. Watch the fingers of the glove: they should point at the ground.
Call 'Up!' and toss one that arrives at the chest. Now the fingers should point at the sky, with the bare hand coming in beside the glove.
If the glove is in the wrong position, do not throw. Hold the ball up, ask 'down or up?', and toss only when the glove is right.
After six called tosses, stop calling and let your child decide. Praise the decision even when the catch is missed.
Keep tosses easy to see: from the front, slow, and never toward the face.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a sock ball and bare hands. Below the waist the pinkies touch and the fingers point down; above the waist the thumbs touch and the fingers point up. The rule is the same.
steps: Child stands in the ready position with a glove on; parent stands 8 feet in front with a soft ball.
Parent calls 'Down!' and tosses a ball that arrives below the belt. Child turns the glove fingers-down and catches.
Child flips the ball back underhand and resets.
Parent calls 'Up!' and tosses a ball that arrives at the chest. Child turns the glove fingers-up with the bare hand alongside.
Repeat six called tosses, alternating down and up.
Parent stops calling and mixes the heights; child decides down or up before the ball arrives.
Finish with three low balls in a row, since fingers-down is the harder habit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove stays fingers-up on a low ball and the ball rolls under it.
commonMistakes.fix: Toss five low balls in a row and have the child touch the ground with the glove fingers before each one arrives.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching a chest-high ball with the glove upside down, palm facing the ground.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child hold the glove up like a stop sign before you toss, thumb toward the nose.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove flips over or closes before the ball gets there.
commonMistakes.fix: Say 'let the ball close the glove' and toss so slowly that squeezing early is obviously too soon.

commonMistakes.mistake: Looking at the parent's face instead of the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child point at the ball with the bare hand while it travels, then catch.

cues: Let the ball close the glove
safety: Soft safety balls only for ages 4-8; this lesson produces a lot of misses on purpose, and misses should not hurt.
Toss from the front and keep every ball below the shoulders at this age.
Make sure the glove fits; a too-large glove cannot be turned fingers-down by a small wrist.

progression.easier: Toss only low balls for a whole session, then only high balls the next, and combine them a week later.
progression.harder: Toss from 15 feet with no calls, and add balls to the glove side and the bare-hand side so the glove has to turn and reach.

items.title: Fielding Footwork: Right-Left-Field and Approach Angles
items.objective: The player will be able to approach a ground ball on a curved path, field it in the triangle, and step right-left toward the target before throwing.
items.summary: Good infielders field with their feet. This lesson teaches the curved approach that puts the body behind the ball and the right-left footwork that turns a catch into a throw.

video.note: The production video will show an overhead drone angle of an 11-year-old shortstop taking a banana-shaped path to a ground ball, then a ground-level slow-motion clip of the right-left footwork into the throw with each step labeled.

explanation: A ground ball is not fielded where it is hit; it is fielded where the fielder meets it. The path the feet take to that meeting point decides whether the body ends up behind the ball or beside it. Beginners run straight at the ball on a line. Experienced infielders take a curved path, often called a banana route, so that the last two or three steps come forward and slightly toward the throwing side.

Why the curve? Momentum. If the final steps are moving toward first base, the throw starts with the body already headed that way. If the final steps are moving sideways, the fielder has to stop, re-balance, and start again, which costs a full second and often produces a weak throw. Fielding through the ball, instead of to it, is the whole idea.

The approach has three speeds. As the ball comes off the bat, the fielder moves fast to get on the curved path. As the fielder nears the ball, the steps shorten and the body lowers into the triangle. The last step before the catch is a small one, timed so the ball arrives just as the glove touches the ground out in front.

Now the footwork after the catch. For a right-handed thrower, funnel the ball to the belly while the right foot steps in front of the left, pointing the toes toward the target. Then the left foot steps directly at the target so the front shoulder points there too, and the throw follows. Coaches say it as 'right, left, throw.' A left-handed thrower mirrors it: left, right, throw.

Keep the steps short and quick, and keep the body low through them. Standing straight up between the catch and the first step is the most common fault, because it wastes time and throws the balance off. The fielder should feel like a wave: low to field, rising smoothly through the steps, and tall only at the release.
parentInstructions: Set two cones or shoes 15 feet apart and stand 30 to 40 feet in front of them with tennis balls or soft balls. Your child starts 10 feet behind the cones, in the middle.
Roll a firm ground ball toward one cone. Watch your child's path: it should curve so the last steps come forward toward you, not straight sideways.
After the catch, watch the feet, not the ball. For a right-hander you want right foot in front, then left foot toward you, then the throw.
Have your child say the words out loud as they move: 'field, right, left, throw.' Saying it keeps the order right.
Catch the throw at your chest. If you have to reach, tell them which way it missed; the front foot usually pointed that way.
Roll no harder than your child can field cleanly. The footwork falls apart when the ball is too fast.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Practice the four-word footwork with no ball at all, stepping over a shoe on the ground. Then add a sock ball rolled by a parent and jog it back instead of throwing.
steps: Shadow the footwork first with no ball: triangle over a shoe, 'field', 'right', 'left', 'throw'. Ten slow reps.
Set two cones 15 feet apart; child starts 10 feet behind them in the ready position.
Parent rolls a ground ball toward the left cone. Child takes a curved path so the last steps come forward.
Child fields in the triangle, funnels to the belly, steps right-left toward the parent, and throws to the chest.
Parent rolls to the right cone. Child curves again so the body ends up behind the ball.
Alternate sides for eight balls, then mix them up so the child must read the direction.
Child resets behind the cones after every throw.
Finish with three easy rolls straight ahead, concentrating only on the right-left steps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running straight sideways and reaching for the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a cone 5 feet behind the ball's path and make the child run around the outside of it before fielding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing straight up after the catch, then starting the feet.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold a hand at the height of the child's head in the triangle and ask them to stay under it through the first step.

commonMistakes.mistake: Feet in the wrong order, left before right for a right-hander.
commonMistakes.fix: Say the words 'right, left, throw' together out loud for ten reps with no ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Final step pointed off to the side so the throw sails.
commonMistakes.fix: Lay a stick on the ground pointing at the target and have the front foot land along it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Approaching too fast and overrunning the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask for small, choppy steps in the last 6 feet, like tiptoeing up to a sleeping dog.

cues: Round it, don't reach for it
safety: Tennis balls or soft balls in a backyard; firm grounders with a hard baseball belong on a groomed field.
The throws in this lesson are real throws. Play five minutes of easy catch first and stop at about 20 throws.
Check the ground for holes and sprinkler heads where the child will be running curved paths.

progression.easier: Remove the throw entirely and have the child field, step right-left, and hand the ball to a parent who walks over.
progression.harder: Roll harder and farther to each side, add a timer, and require a chest-high throw to a partner 60 feet away.

items.title: Backhand Fundamentals
items.objective: The player will be able to field a ground ball hit to the throwing-hand side by crossing over, planting the back foot, and catching with the glove thumb-down and fingers-down.
items.summary: The backhand is the play on the ball hit to the throwing-arm side, where the glove has to reach across the body. Learn the cross-over step, the plant, and the thumb-down glove that make it routine.

video.note: The production video will show a slow-motion backhand by a 12-year-old third baseman from the side and from behind, highlighting the cross-over step, the planted right foot, and the glove with thumb pointing down.

explanation: Some ground balls are hit too far to the throwing-hand side to get in front of. For a right-handed fielder that means a ball to the right, toward third base from the shortstop spot. The play is called a backhand because the glove hand reaches across the body with the back of the hand leading. It feels awkward at first, which is exactly why it needs its own lesson.

The footwork starts with a cross-over step. The fielder pivots on the throwing-side foot and swings the glove-side foot across in front of it, turning the hips toward the ball. Running sideways with shuffle steps is too slow for a backhand; the cross-over covers ground.

As the fielder arrives at the ball, the throwing-side foot plants firmly on the ground, slightly ahead of the ball, and the knee bends deeply. For a right-hander that is the right foot. Planting on that foot does two jobs: it stops the body from drifting past the ball, and it loads the leg that will push the throw back toward first base.

Now the glove. The glove hand drops low with the thumb pointing at the ground and the fingers pointing down, so the pocket faces the oncoming ball like a wall. The elbow stays slightly bent and relaxed. The bare hand cannot reach across to help on a true backhand, so the fielder must watch the ball all the way into the pocket, head down, and squeeze.

After the catch, the fielder rises, turns the shoulders toward the target, and steps with the glove-side foot into the throw. Young players should not worry about the dramatic jump-throw seen on television. A balanced plant, a clean catch, and a strong step are the goal, and the throw can even be a little late at first while the catch becomes reliable.
parentInstructions: Kneel 15 to 20 feet from your child, but offset toward their glove side, so your rolls travel across the body toward the throwing hand. For a right-handed child, you kneel to their left and roll toward their right.
Roll slowly at first, only two steps to the throwing side. The child's job is to cross over, plant the back foot, and show you a thumb-down glove.
Watch the glove as the ball arrives. If you can see the back of your child's hand, the glove is tilted and the ball will roll off. You should see the full pocket facing you.
Ask your child to keep the head down until the ball is squeezed. Lifting the head early is the number one cause of a backhand miss.
Have the ball flipped back to you underhand. The throw is a separate skill and this lesson is about the catch.
Soft balls or tennis balls only; a hard baseball skipping past an unprotected backhand side can hit the ribs.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a tennis ball and have the child field it bare-handed with the thumb turned down and palm facing the ball. The hand learns the same shape the glove must make.
steps: Child starts in the ready position; parent kneels 15 to 20 feet away, offset to the glove side.
Parent rolls slowly two steps toward the child's throwing-hand side.
Child pivots on the throwing-side foot and crosses the glove-side foot over in front of it.
Child plants the throwing-side foot just ahead of the ball and bends that knee deeply.
Glove drops with thumb down and fingers down; eyes stay on the ball until it is squeezed in the pocket.
Child rises, turns the shoulders toward the parent, and flips the ball back underhand.
After six clean backhands, parent rolls a medium-speed ball three steps away.
Finish with three easy balls straight ahead so the body remembers the normal triangle too.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shuffling sideways instead of crossing over, so the ball gets past.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a cone a step to the throwing side and have the child step over it with the glove-side foot before every roll.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove tilted so the back of the hand faces the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice ten dry reps where the child shows you the pocket like a stop sign held low, thumb at the ground.

commonMistakes.mistake: Head lifts toward the target before the catch.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask the child to read a letter you wrote on the ball before squeezing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drifting past the ball because the back foot never plants.
commonMistakes.fix: Draw a chalk line where the plant foot should stop and have them freeze on it for one second after the catch.

safety: Soft balls or tennis balls at home; the backhand leaves the body exposed, and a hard ball off the ribs hurts.
On a driveway, face the child toward the garage so missed balls do not roll into the street.
Stretch the legs lightly first; the deep knee bend on a plant foot surprises kids who have not warmed up.

progression.easier: Place the ball on the ground in the backhand spot and let the child walk through the cross-over and plant before picking it up.
progression.harder: Roll harder from 30 feet, require a full right-left-throw to a target 60 feet away, and alternate backhands with normal grounders so the child must read the ball.

items.title: Forehand and Glove-Side Plays
items.objective: The player will be able to field a ground ball to the glove side by planting the glove-side foot outside the ball, catching out front, and pushing back toward the target to throw.
items.summary: Balls hit to the glove side look easy but produce rushed, off-line throws. This lesson teaches the plant-and-push forehand that turns momentum back toward the base.

video.note: The production video will show a 10-year-old second baseman fielding forehand ground balls, with freeze frames on the planted left foot, the glove reaching out front, and the push-off back toward first base.

explanation: A forehand is any ground ball the fielder reaches with the glove while moving toward the glove side. For a right-handed fielder that is a ball to the left, toward second base from the shortstop spot or toward first base from second. The glove is on the correct side, so the catch itself is natural. The trouble is that the body is running away from the target, and the throw has to come back the other way.

The solution is the plant. As the fielder reaches the ball, the glove-side foot lands on the far side of the ball, past it, with the knee bent. For a right-hander that is the left foot. The ball is then fielded in front of that planted foot, with the glove fingers pointing down and the pocket facing the ball. That foot is now a wall that stops the body from sliding farther away from the target.

From the plant, the fielder pushes. The weight shifts off the planted foot and back toward the target, usually with a small hop onto the throwing-side foot. The shoulders turn so the glove-side shoulder points at the base. Then the glove-side foot steps toward the target and the throw is made. Plant, push, step, throw.

The glove reaches but the body does not stretch. Many kids extend the arm as far as it will go while the feet stop early, and they field the ball with a straight arm and a tilted glove. The feet should carry the fielder close enough that the glove reaches out comfortably, elbow slightly bent, with the bare hand ready to cover the ball.

On a ball hit very hard to the glove side, there is not time for the full plant and push; the fielder catches it, stops with whatever foot is available, and throws. That is fine. The plant-and-push is the routine play, and routine plays are the ones that win Little League games.
parentInstructions: Stand 30 to 40 feet from your child, offset toward their glove side, with soft balls. A target (you, a sibling, or an empty bucket) goes where first base would be, 40 feet to the throwing side.
Roll a ground ball three steps to the glove side, slow enough that your child can get there with two shuffle steps and a reach.
Watch the glove-side foot. It should land past the ball, so the ball is fielded in front of that foot, not beside it.
After the catch, watch for the push back toward the target. If your child keeps drifting away from the target while throwing, the plant did not happen.
Catch the throw at your chest if you are the target, and tell your child whether it tailed toward the drift side.
Keep rolls to the glove side only for this lesson. Mixing in backhands comes later, once the plant is automatic.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a tennis ball across grass and have the child field it bare-handed, plant, push back, and jog the ball to you. The feet are learning, so the throw can wait.
steps: Child in the ready position; parent 30 to 40 feet away, offset to the glove side, with a target set up toward first base.
Parent rolls a ball three steps to the glove side.
Child shuffles two steps, then reaches with the glove, fingers down, while the glove-side foot plants on the far side of the ball.
Child fields the ball in front of the planted foot, bare hand covering.
Child pushes off the planted foot, hops onto the throwing-side foot, and turns the shoulders toward the target.
Child steps with the glove-side foot at the target and throws to the chest.
Child jogs back and resets; the next roll goes one step farther.
After six, finish with three gentle rolls so the last throws are strong and on line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fielding beside the foot instead of in front of it, so the body is still moving away.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a cone where the ball will arrive and have the child plant the foot past the cone before the ball reaches it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching with a straight arm because the feet stopped early.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask for one more shuffle step than feels necessary, then a relaxed reach.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing while still drifting, so the ball sails to the drift side.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child freeze on the planted foot for a count of one, then push and throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing up tall during the push so the throw loses power.
commonMistakes.fix: Tell the child to keep the chest over the knees until the step toward the target.

safety: Soft balls in a backyard; hard baseballs only on a field with good footing.
Play easy catch first, because these throws follow a change of direction and need warm muscles.
Keep the target off to the side of the rolling lane so a wild throw cannot hit the roller.

progression.easier: Roll only two steps away and let the child plant, push, and hand the ball to a parent standing at the target spot.
progression.harder: Roll harder and farther, mix forehands with straight-on grounders, and have the target call for the throw at the chest or at the knees.

items.title: The Transfer: Glove to Hand Quickly
items.objective: The player will be able to move the ball from the glove to the throwing hand at the belly in one quick, clean motion and come up with a four-seam grip.
items.summary: The transfer is the hidden half-second between the catch and the throw. Learn to make it clean and automatic, and every throw after a catch gets faster.

video.note: The production video will show slow-motion close-ups of an 8-year-old's hands pulling a caught ball to the belly and popping it into the throwing hand, ending with the four-seam grip shown to the camera.

explanation: Between the catch and the throw there is a small move that nobody notices unless it goes wrong: getting the ball out of the glove and into the throwing hand. Coaches call it the transfer. A slow transfer makes a fast fielder look slow, and a fumbled transfer turns an easy out into a runner standing on first base.

The transfer happens at the belly, not out in front and not up by the shoulder. After the catch, both hands pull in to the belly button together. There the glove tips sideways and the bare hand reaches in to take the ball. Because the hands are close to the body, the eyes can glance at the ball if they need to and the arms are already in position to start the throw.

Do not dig. If the ball is buried deep in the pocket, the fingers have to fish for it, which is slow. Catch the ball in the webbing or shallow part of the pocket with the bare hand covering, and the glove can almost hand the ball to the throwing hand. Soft hands that do not squeeze the glove shut around the ball make this possible.

The grip matters too. As the bare hand takes the ball, the fingers find a seam and settle into a four-seam grip, with the index and middle fingers across the horseshoe of the seams and the thumb underneath. Good players do this by feel in a fraction of a second, and the only way to get there is hundreds of repetitions with a ball in the hand, which can happen on the couch with a sock ball.

Finally, link the hands to the feet. While the transfer is happening at the belly, the right foot is already stepping in front of the left for a right-handed thrower. Hands and feet move at the same time, and the ball comes out of the transfer just as the left foot lands pointing at the target.
parentInstructions: Begin with no partner: give your child a sock ball or soft ball and a glove and have them toss it a few inches up, catch with two hands, and pull it to the belly to transfer. Ten of those before you throw anything.
Stand 15 feet away and toss easy chest-high balls. Your only job is to watch the hands after the catch: both to the belly, then the ball pops into the throwing hand.
Ask to see the grip. After each transfer your child holds the ball up by the ear and shows you two fingers across the seams before tossing back.
Count out loud how long the transfer takes: 'one' should be the catch, 'two' should be the ball in the throwing hand. If you get to 'three,' slow the tosses down and rebuild.
Once the hands are smooth, add the feet: right foot then left foot toward you as the hands transfer, for a right-hander.
Keep sessions to about eight minutes. This skill improves through many short visits, not one long one.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A sock ball and bare hands work completely. Catch in the non-throwing hand with the throwing hand covering, pull to the belly, and pass the ball to the throwing hand. No glove is needed to learn the rhythm.
steps: Child holds a sock ball in the glove and tosses it six inches up, catching it back in the glove with the bare hand covering.
Both hands pull to the belly button and the ball pops into the throwing hand.
Child shows the four-seam grip up by the ear, puts the ball back in the glove, and repeats ten times.
Parent stands 15 feet away and tosses easy chest-high soft balls.
Child catches with two hands, transfers at the belly, shows the grip, and tosses back.
After ten clean transfers, child adds right-left footwork toward the parent while the hands work.
Parent speeds up the tosses slightly so there is a reason to be quick.
Finish with five knee-high tosses so the fingers-down catch flows into the same transfer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Transferring out in front of the body with arms extended.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child touch the belly button with both hands before the ball changes hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Digging the ball out of a deep pocket.
commonMistakes.fix: Catch with the bare hand covering so the ball stays shallow, and loosen the squeeze on the glove.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing hand hangs at the side during the catch.
commonMistakes.fix: Hold both hands up in front of the chest before each toss, like getting ready to clap.

commonMistakes.mistake: No grip, so the throw comes out sideways.
commonMistakes.fix: Pause after each transfer and show the parent two fingers across the seams before tossing back.

cues: Two hands in, one hand out
safety: Soft safety balls for ages 7-8; a drill that speeds up the hands produces drops, and drops with a hard ball bruise toes and shins.
In a garage or small room, use a sock ball and keep tosses low and slow.
Stop the drill if the child starts snatching at the ball in frustration; fast only comes after smooth.

progression.easier: Remove the partner and the glove and do sock-ball transfers only, hand to hand at the belly, while sitting on the floor.
progression.harder: Toss low and to both sides, require the right-left footwork on every catch, and time 30-second rounds for a record number of clean transfers.

items.title: Funnel and Throw: Fielding Into Throwing in One Motion
items.objective: The player will be able to field a ground ball, funnel it to the belly, step right-left, and throw to a target in one continuous motion with no pause.
items.summary: The best infielders look like they catch and throw in one piece. This lesson connects the triangle, the funnel, the transfer, and the footwork into a single smooth play.

video.note: The production video will show a 12-year-old fielding ground balls at full speed, first in real time and then slowed down, with a moving highlight that follows the ball from the glove to the belly to the release.

explanation: Up to now the pieces of a ground ball have been learned one at a time: the triangle, watching the ball in, the transfer, and the right-left steps. In a game they are not pieces at all. The ball comes in, the body rises, the feet move, and the throw leaves, all as one wave. The word coaches use for the first part of that wave is the funnel.

The funnel is the pull. The ball enters the glove out in front of the body, the bare hand closes over it, and both hands draw back toward the belly button along a straight line. Think of pouring the ball down a funnel into the middle of the body. As the hands travel, the knees straighten a little and the chest rises, so by the time the ball reaches the belly the fielder is already standing taller and starting to turn.

There is no stop at the belly. The transfer happens while the right foot is stepping in front of the left, for a right-handed thrower, and the ball is coming out of the glove as that foot lands. The left foot then steps straight at the target and the arm follows. Left-handers do the mirror image. Catch-step-step-throw should feel like four beats of one rhythm, not four separate tasks.

A good test is to listen. A fielder who stops has a gap of silence between the catch and the first footstep. A fielder who funnels has footsteps that start almost the instant the ball hits the glove. Parents can hear the difference even if they cannot yet see it.

Accuracy comes from the front foot and the fingers. The last step points at the target, and the fingers stay on top of the ball at release so the throw has backspin and carries straight. A hurried throw with the fingers on the side of the ball will tail away from the first baseman, so even at full speed the funnel should end with a clean four-seam grip.
parentInstructions: You will need a target besides yourself: a second adult, a sibling with a glove, or a bucket set on its side. Put the target 40 to 45 feet to your child's throwing side, where first base would be. Stand 20 feet in front of your child with the balls.
Roll a medium-speed ground ball straight at your child. Watch the hands come to the belly and the feet start at the same time; a visible pause means the play is still in pieces.
Listen for the footsteps. If there is silence between the catch and the first step, say 'no stop' and roll the next one slower.
The target calls 'good' only for a throw caught without moving the feet. Anything else is just a throw.
Build speed slowly across the session: easy rolls for the first five, medium for the next ten, and a few firm ones only if everything is clean.
Fifteen throws is enough for one session; this lesson is about rhythm, not volume.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a tennis ball to the child and have them funnel, step right-left, and throw the tennis ball back at your glove-side shoulder from 30 feet. A tennis ball is light enough to do this safely in a yard.
steps: Set a target 40 to 45 feet to the child's throwing side; parent stands 20 feet in front with balls.
Child sets up in the ready position and the parent rolls a medium ground ball straight on.
Child drops into the triangle, watches the ball in, and covers it with the bare hand.
Both hands funnel to the belly while the body rises and the right foot steps in front of the left.
Ball transfers to the throwing hand as that foot lands; left foot steps at the target.
Child throws to the target's chest with fingers on top of the ball.
Target calls 'good' or stays quiet; child resets to the ready position.
Repeat for three rounds of five, rolling slightly harder each round only if the rhythm holds.

commonMistakes.mistake: A full stop at the belly before the feet begin.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child say 'catch' and 'step' out loud, with no word allowed in between.

commonMistakes.mistake: Rising straight up before funneling, so the ball is caught high and bobbled.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask them to keep the glove touching the ground until the ball arrives, then funnel.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing without a grip because the hands are rushing.
commonMistakes.fix: Slow the roll down and have them show the parent the grip at the ear for five reps before throwing again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Front foot pointed toward the roller instead of the target.
commonMistakes.fix: Place a glove on the ground pointing at the target and have the front foot land beside it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throw tails away from the target because fingers are on the side of the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the four-seam grip after the funnel and have the child finish with the fingers pulling down through the ball.

safety: These are game-speed throws. Play easy catch for five minutes first and keep the session to about 15 throws.
Soft balls for 9-year-olds new to the drill; hard baseballs only on a field with a target who catches well.
Put the target off to the side of the rolling lane so a high throw never travels toward the roller.

progression.easier: Roll softly from 15 feet and have the child funnel and step right-left, then simply hand the ball to a parent who steps in; add the throw later.
progression.harder: Roll to both sides, add a stopwatch from the roll to the catch at the target, and run it as a line with teammates at practice.

items.title: Catching Fly Balls: Getting Under the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to track a softly tossed pop-up, move the feet so the ball comes down in front of the face, and catch it above the head with two hands and fingers up.
items.summary: Pop-ups scare more young players than ground balls do. This lesson uses short, soft underhand tosses to teach kids to move their feet under the ball and catch it with two hands.

video.note: The production video will show a parent tossing a soft safety ball underhand to a 6-year-old from 8 feet, with a slow-motion side view of the ball peaking above the child's head and the child's feet adjusting before the hands go up.

explanation: A ball in the air is harder for a young child than a ball on the ground for one reason: it moves in two directions at once, up and then down, while also coming toward them. The eyes have to track a curve. The good news is that the curve is predictable, and with enough gentle repetitions the brain learns where the ball will land before it gets there.

The first skill is getting under the ball. The child should move the feet so that the ball would hit them on the forehead if they did nothing. That spot, slightly in front of the face and above the eyes, is where a pop-up is easiest to see and catch. A child who stands still and reaches to the side has to guess, and guesses get dropped.

The hands go up late, not early. Teach the child to find the ball with the eyes, move the feet, and only then raise the hands to a spot just above and in front of the forehead. Hands that go up the moment the ball is tossed block the view and lock the feet in place.

Catch with two hands. The glove is open with the fingers pointing at the sky, and the bare hand sits beside it with the thumbs close together, ready to trap the ball once it lands in the pocket. Younger children can make a basket with two bare hands at chest height and let the ball drop in, which builds tracking without any fear of a glove.

At ages 4 to 6 the toss is a soft safety ball or a sock ball lobbed underhand from 6 to 8 feet so it peaks a foot or two above the head and comes down slowly. Ages 7 to 8 can handle a higher toss from a little farther away once they are catching cleanly. Real fly balls on a field, thrown or hit, come at age 9 and up in the drop-step lesson.
parentInstructions: Stand 6 to 8 feet in front of your child with a soft safety ball or a sock ball. Check overhead for branches, wires, and basketball hoops.

Toss underhand with a smooth swing of the arm so the ball peaks a foot or two above your child's head and drops softly toward the hands. A good toss falls almost straight down at the end; a bad one flies at the face.
Say 'Up!' as you release so the eyes find the ball right away.
Watch the feet before the hands. If the child reaches without moving, toss the next one a little shorter so the ball comes right to them, and build the distance back one toss at a time.
Watch the eyes. A child who shuts the eyes or turns the head is scared, not uncoordinated. Lower the toss until the eyes stay open and never go faster than the eyes can handle.
Have the ball tossed back underhand. Ten tosses, a break, ten more, and stop while it is still fun.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A rolled-up pair of socks is the best first pop-up ball: it floats down slowly and cannot hurt. Catch it in two bare hands with the thumbs together, like a basket.
steps: Child stands with feet apart and hands by the chin; parent stands 6 to 8 feet in front with a soft ball.
Parent says 'Up!' and tosses underhand so the ball peaks just above the child's head.
Child watches the ball and moves the feet so it is coming down in front of the face.
Hands go up late: glove fingers to the sky, bare hand beside it, thumbs close together.
Child catches, squeezes with both hands, and pulls the ball down to the chest.
Child tosses it back underhand and resets.
After five catches in a row, parent tosses one a step to the left, then one a step to the right.
For 7-8 year olds catching easily, parent backs up to 12 feet and tosses a little higher.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands go up right away and block the view.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child keep the hands by the chin until you say 'now,' which you say as the ball starts coming down.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reaching to the side instead of moving the feet.
commonMistakes.fix: Toss every ball a half step off center and insist the feet move first; say 'feet, then hands.'

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching with the glove alone and the ball popping out.
commonMistakes.fix: Go back to bare-hand basket catches with a sock ball for a round, then add the glove with the bare hand helping.

commonMistakes.mistake: Turning the head away or closing the eyes.
commonMistakes.fix: Lower the toss height until the eyes stay open, then raise it a few inches at a time over several sessions.

cues: Catch it in front of your face
safety: Soft safety balls or sock balls only for pop-ups at ages 4-8; a hard baseball coming down on a small face is not worth the risk.
Toss the ball so it drops to the hands rather than flying at the child; a toss that drifts toward the face teaches flinching.
Check the sky for branches, wires, and hoops before the first toss, and keep siblings out of the landing zone.

progression.easier: Toss a sock ball from 4 feet so it peaks at the child's chin height, and let them catch it in two bare hands against the chest.
progression.harder: Back up to 15 feet, toss so the ball peaks 6 to 8 feet above the head, and add tosses two steps to each side.

items.title: Fly Balls: The Drop Step and Angles
items.objective: The player will be able to take a drop step on a fly ball hit over the head, run on an angle to a spot behind the ball, and catch it while moving forward.
items.summary: Balls hit over an outfielder's head are the hardest plays in youth baseball. This lesson teaches the drop step, the angled route, and the habit of catching the ball while moving forward.

video.note: The production video will show a 10-year-old outfielder taking drop steps to both sides on fly balls thrown by a coach, filmed from behind so the first step and the angled route are easy to see, with a wrong-way example of backpedaling for comparison.

explanation: An outfielder who backpedals on a deep fly ball is in trouble. Running backward is slow, it is easy to trip, and the ball often sails over the glove anyway. The fix is the drop step: on a ball hit over the head, the foot on the side the ball is going steps straight back, the hips open toward that side, and the fielder turns and runs like a sprinter.

Reading the ball comes first. In the first half-second after contact, the fielder watches the ball leave the bat and decides: in front of me, or over my head? For anything over the head, the drop step happens immediately, before the fielder is sure exactly where it will land. It is far easier to come back in on a ball than to go back on one.

The route is an angle, not a straight line and not a curve. The fielder picks a spot behind where the ball will land and runs toward that spot on the balls of the feet, glove hand down at the side. Running with the glove up in the air slows the legs and bounces the vision. The glove goes up only in the last two or three steps.

Catching the ball while moving forward is the goal. If the fielder gets behind the ball, the final steps come toward the infield, the body is balanced, and the momentum is already headed where the throw needs to go. A catch made while drifting backward usually becomes a weak throw and an extra base for the runner.

The catch itself is above the throwing-side shoulder with two hands, so the ball is already near the ear when the throw starts. After the catch comes a crow hop, which is a small hop onto the throwing-side foot that gathers the body before a long throw, and then a throw to the cutoff man, the infielder who comes out to meet the throw. Ages 9 and up practice this with real fly balls thrown by a coach on a field; younger players stay with soft tosses.
parentInstructions: You need open space: a park or a field with at least 90 feet of room behind your child. Walk the grass first and move anything a running child could trip on.

Stand 40 feet in front of your child. Point to a side, then throw a fly ball over their head toward that side. For a 9-year-old start with a soft safety ball thrown high and easy; an 11-year-old can take a real baseball.
Watch only the first step. It should be straight back with the foot on the side the ball is going, with the hips turning. A hop in place or a step forward is the thing to correct.
Watch the glove while your child runs. It should be down at the side until the last two or three steps.
Watch the direction of the last steps. Forward is the goal; drifting backward means the drop step was late or the route was too shallow.
Have the ball thrown to a partner or rolled into a bucket 60 feet away, not back to you at 40 feet. After 12 throws, stop; these are long throws.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Throw a tennis ball by hand over the child's head in a park and have them jog the ball back instead of throwing it. The drop step and the angled route are learned exactly the same way.
steps: Child starts at a cone with the parent 40 feet in front; a cutoff partner or bucket waits about 60 feet to the side.
Parent points left or right, then throws a fly ball over the child's head to that side.
Child drop-steps with the foot on that side, opens the hips, and runs on an angle to a spot behind the ball.
Glove stays down while running and comes up in the last two or three steps.
Child catches above the throwing-side shoulder with two hands while moving forward.
Child crow hops and throws to the cutoff partner's chest, or rolls the ball into the bucket.
Child jogs back to the cone and goes the other direction on the next ball.
After eight balls, parent stops pointing so the child has to read the ball off the hand.

commonMistakes.mistake: Backpedaling instead of turning and running.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child start with their back half-turned to you so the only option is to run; then square them up again.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hopping in place or stepping forward before the drop step.
commonMistakes.fix: Say 'back foot first' before every throw and reward the first step, not the catch.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running with the glove up, which slows the legs.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child carry the glove at the hip like a holster until you yell 'glove!' in the last steps.

commonMistakes.mistake: Route too shallow, so the ball sails over the glove.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a cone 10 feet beyond the landing spot and have the child run to the cone before coming back to the ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catching while drifting backward and throwing weakly.
commonMistakes.fix: Throw shorter so the child can get behind the ball easily, then stretch the distance one throw at a time.

cues: Drop the foot, open the hip
Get behind it, catch it coming in
safety: Long throws to the cutoff require a warmed-up arm; play catch first and stop at about 12 throws.
Walk the running lane before the first ball and move bags, cones, sprinkler heads, and younger siblings.
Soft safety balls for 9-10 year olds until they track balls over the head confidently; a hard ball off the head is a real injury.
Teach the child to shout 'ball!' and let it drop rather than catch anything they lose in the sun.

progression.easier: Throw shorter fly balls that land only a few steps behind the child, and call the side early so the only new skill is the first step.
progression.harder: Stop calling the side, throw deeper and more to the sides, and add a live runner tagging up from third so the throw has to beat someone.

items.title: Communication: Calling the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to call for a fly ball loudly and early, and to answer a teammate's call by backing off and covering behind them.
items.summary: Two fielders chasing one pop-up end up with a collision or a dropped ball. This lesson teaches the words, the timing, and the backup job that keep everyone safe and the ball in a glove.

video.note: The production video will show two 9-year-olds converging on a pop-up, one calling 'Mine!' three times while the ball is still rising and the other answering 'Take it!' and peeling off behind, with a second clip of what a silent, near-collision play looks like.

explanation: When a pop-up goes into the air between two fielders, both of them want it, and both of them are being good teammates by trying. The danger is that neither one knows what the other is doing. Communication is the fix: one fielder claims the ball out loud, the other gives it up out loud, and everybody knows the plan before the ball comes down.

The words are simple. The fielder who wants the ball yells 'Mine, mine, mine!' three times, loud enough for the whole infield to hear. Three times matters because one shout can be missed in the noise of a game. The other fielder answers 'Take it, take it!' so the first fielder knows the call was heard. Some teams use 'I got it' or 'Ball, ball, ball'; any words work as long as the whole team uses the same ones.

Timing is the hard part. The call has to come while the ball is still going up, not as it comes down. A late call gives the other fielder no time to stop, and two players stopping at the same moment leaves the ball on the grass. Teach children to decide quickly, call early, and live with the result even if the other player was slightly closer.

The player who gives up the ball still has a job. That player peels off to a spot about ten feet behind the fielder making the catch, in line with the ball, ready to grab anything that bounces off the glove. Backing up is not quitting on the play; it is the second half of the play.

Priorities help when two calls happen at once. Most teams teach that the center fielder outranks the other outfielders, outfielders outrank infielders on balls between them, and the shortstop outranks the other infielders. Coaches set these rules for their own teams and the details can vary, so players should learn their team's version at practice and use it every time.
parentInstructions: This lesson needs at least three people: a tosser and two fielders. Two siblings or a neighbor and a parent are perfect.
Stand 25 feet in front of two fielders who are 20 feet apart. Toss a soft ball high into the space between them. For 7-8 year olds an underhand toss that peaks about 10 feet up is plenty.
Listen for the call while the ball is still going up. If you hear nothing until the ball is coming down, stop and ask, 'Who had it?' and toss again.
Listen for the answer. The second fielder must say 'Take it!' and move behind the first; silence from the second fielder is a mistake even when the catch is made.
Praise the loudest early call more than the catch. The skill being taught is the talking.
Mix in a few tosses obviously closer to one fielder so both children practice calling fast when the answer is easy.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A sock ball tossed by hand works for two kids and a parent in a living room with a high ceiling or a yard. The words and the timing are the lesson; the ball barely matters.
steps: Two fielders stand 20 feet apart facing the tosser, who stands 25 feet in front.
Tosser lobs a high pop-up between the two fielders.
Both fielders move toward the ball; the one who sees it best yells 'Mine! Mine! Mine!' while it is still rising.
The other fielder yells 'Take it! Take it!' and peels off to a spot 10 feet behind the catcher.
The caller catches with two hands and flips the ball back to the tosser.
If nobody called, the ball does not count even if it was caught, and the tosser repeats it.
After six pop-ups, the fielders switch sides so each one practices calling from both spots.
Finish with three tosses clearly closer to one fielder to practice fast, obvious calls.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling too late, as the ball is already coming down.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the tosser count 'one, two' after release; the call must be heard by 'two' or the ball is re-tossed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Both fielders call and neither gives way.
commonMistakes.fix: Teach the team priority rule and have the lower-priority player practice saying 'Take it!' even when they wanted the ball.

commonMistakes.mistake: The second fielder stops and watches instead of backing up.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the backup spot a cone 10 feet behind the catcher that the second fielder must touch on every play.

commonMistakes.mistake: Quiet, mumbled calls nobody can hear.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the tosser turn their back and judge only by sound; if the tosser cannot hear it, it did not happen.

cues: Call it early, call it loud
Take it means I'm behind you
safety: Soft safety balls for ages 7-8 and for any group new to the drill, because collisions happen when two kids chase one ball.
Teach the backup fielder to peel off behind the catcher, never beside them, so a late stop does not become a crash.
Keep the toss height modest at first; the goal is talking, not tracking a towering fly ball.

progression.easier: Toss lower, slower pop-ups clearly closer to one fielder and simply practice the words in the right order.
progression.harder: Add a third fielder, throw real fly balls on a field for ages 9 and up, and introduce the team's priority rules for which position outranks which.

items.title: Slow Rollers and Charging the Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to charge a slowly hit ground ball under control, field it with the glove or the bare hand, and throw on the run to first base.
items.summary: A slow roller is a race between the fielder and the runner. This lesson teaches infielders to charge hard but under control, pick the ball cleanly, and throw without stopping.

video.note: The production video will show an 11-year-old third baseman charging slow rollers, with one clip of a glove-side pickup and throw on the run and one clip of a bare-hand scoop on a ball that has stopped, both in slow motion from the side.

explanation: A slow roller is a ground ball hit softly, often off the end of the bat or from a bunt attempt, that takes a long time to reach the fielder. If the fielder waits for it in the ready position, the batter is standing on first base before the throw is made. The only way to make the play is to go get the ball. Infielders call this charging.

Charging means sprinting toward the ball on the balls of the feet, but under control. The first steps are fast. As the fielder closes in, the steps shorten a little so the eyes can read the last hop and the body can get low. The fielder never comes to a full stop, because stopping gives back every bit of time the charge gained.

There are two ways to pick the ball. If it is still rolling, the fielder uses the glove, placing it on the ground just outside the glove-side foot so the ball rolls in while the body keeps moving forward. If the ball has stopped or is barely moving, the fielder bare-hands it, scooping with the fingers underneath the ball and pushing it into the ground slightly so it does not squirt away. Palming the ball from above is the slow way and it fails on wet grass.

The throw comes on the run from a lower arm angle than usual. The fielder plants the glove-side foot toward first base and throws in the same motion as the pickup, almost like skipping a stone. The arm comes through sidearm or even lower, and that is correct for this one play. Coaches who insist on an over-the-top throw here are asking the fielder to stand up and lose the race.

Judgment is part of the skill. A fielder who charges every ball will sometimes get eaten up by a ball that was hit harder than it looked. Players learn to read the speed off the bat in the first step and to charge hardest on bunts, dribblers, and balls that die in the grass.
parentInstructions: Stand where home plate would be with several soft balls. Your child starts 50 feet away, where a third baseman stands. A target (another person or an empty bucket) goes 40 to 60 feet to your child's left, toward first base.
Roll the ball softly so it dies about halfway to your child. Call 'go!' as you release it.
Watch the last three steps of the charge. They should get a little shorter without ever stopping. A dead stop before the pickup is the main thing to fix.
Watch which hand picks the ball: glove if it is still rolling, bare hand if it has stopped. Call out 'glove' or 'hand' as it slows if your child is unsure.
Expect a lower, sidearm-style throw on this play and do not correct it toward over-the-top; that is the right throw for a slow roller.
Run this on grass, not concrete, and warm up with easy catch first. Twelve slow rollers is a full session.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a tennis ball slowly across a lawn and have the child charge, bare-hand it, and jog it to you. The charge and the scoop are the lesson; the throw can be added when a safe target is available.
steps: Child in the ready position 50 feet from the parent; a target set up 40 to 60 feet toward first base.
Parent dribbles a slow roller halfway toward the child and calls 'go!'
Child charges hard on the balls of the feet, shortening the steps as the ball gets close.
If the ball is rolling, child fields it with the glove outside the glove-side foot while still moving.
If the ball has stopped, child scoops it bare-handed with the fingers under the ball.
Child steps toward the target with the glove-side foot and throws on the run from a low arm angle.
Child jogs back to the starting spot and resets.
Alternate rolling balls and stopped balls for twelve total, ending with two easy ones.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping completely before picking up the ball.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child jog through the pickup without a ball three times, then add the ball and keep the same rhythm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Palming a stopped ball from above so it squirts away.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice ten bare-hand scoops of a stationary ball, fingers first, pushing the ball into the ground before lifting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing up tall to throw over the top and losing the race.
commonMistakes.fix: Tell the child the throw on this play comes from the hip, and let them see that it still reaches the target.

commonMistakes.mistake: Charging a ball that was hit too hard and getting handcuffed.
commonMistakes.fix: Mix in a few medium-speed rollers and praise the child for slowing down and setting the triangle on those.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove placed behind the foot so the ball is fielded too late.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a chalk spot just outside the glove-side foot's landing point and have the glove touch it before the ball arrives.

cues: Throw from the hip on the run
safety: Soft balls in a backyard for this lesson, because throwing on the run is learned best with a forgiving ball.
Warm up the arm with easy catch first; low-angle throws on the run put more stress on a cold arm than a standard throw.
Charge on grass only, never on concrete, and check for holes where the child will be sprinting.

progression.easier: Roll the ball so it stops completely and let the child walk through the charge, scoop, and step without a throw.
progression.harder: Add a runner who starts at home when the ball is rolled and races to a cone 60 feet away, so the throw has to beat someone.

items.title: Short Hops: Playing the Hop You Want
items.objective: The player will be able to read the bounces of a ground ball, move the feet to take it on a long hop or a short hop, and field a short hop with the glove out front and soft hands.
items.summary: The in-between hop is the one that handcuffs infielders. This lesson teaches players to choose their hop by moving their feet and to catch short hops cleanly off the ground.

video.note: The production video will show a 12-year-old infielder fielding tossed short hops in slow motion, with the glove reaching out to meet the ball right after the bounce, plus a side-by-side of a long hop, a short hop, and an in-between hop with each labeled.

explanation: A ground ball bounces, and each bounce gives the fielder three choices. The long hop is caught at the top of a bounce or on its way down, when the ball is easy to see. The short hop is caught just after the ball hits the ground, before it has a chance to rise. The in-between hop is caught at the ball's rising middle, where it is changing height the fastest and is hardest to judge. Good infielders avoid the in-between hop at all costs.

You cannot control where the ball bounces, but you can control where you are standing when it does. Moving a step forward turns an in-between hop into a short hop. Staying back a step turns it into a long hop. This is why infielders read the first two bounces as they approach and then adjust the final steps, creeping in or holding ground, to pick the hop they want.

The short hop is the one that needs its own technique, because many kids fear it. The secret is that a short hop is actually easy if the glove is out in front of the body. The glove reaches toward the ball, fingers down, and catches it inches after the bounce, before it can jump. If the glove waits back near the body, the ball has time to rise and it eats the fielder up at the chest or chin.

Soft hands matter more here than anywhere else. The arm stays relaxed, the wrist is loose, and as the ball arrives the hands give back slightly toward the body, which takes the sting out and keeps the ball from popping out. A stiff arm and a stabbing motion is what turns a short hop into a bruise.

Wall ball is the best way to learn hops at home. A tennis ball thrown against a garage door comes back as a grounder, a short hop, or a line drive depending on where it hits the wall, and the player gets hundreds of hops in a few minutes without anyone to roll them. Tennis balls only; anything harder comes back too fast off a wall at close range.
parentInstructions: Start with tosses, not a wall. Kneel 10 to 12 feet from your child with a tennis ball and toss it so it bounces once, about 2 feet in front of the glove. That is a short hop.
Watch the glove. It should reach out toward the bounce, fingers down, and catch the ball right off the ground. A glove that stays back by the knees means the ball will jump up at the chest.
Watch the arm. A locked elbow and a stab are the problem; you want a relaxed arm that gives back a little as the ball arrives.

Toss some long hops that bounce 6 feet in front and let your child catch them high. Then toss in-between hops that bounce 4 feet in front and have your child step forward to turn them into short hops.
Move to wall ball only after the tossed short hops are clean. Set up 10 to 12 feet from a garage door, tennis ball only, and let your child throw softly at the base of the wall.
Check the wall surface first; wooden doors dent and some painted surfaces scuff. Never play wall ball near windows.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A parent can toss a sock ball so it bounces once in front of bare hands on a hard floor. It will not bounce much, which is fine for learning the reach-out-front habit.
steps: Child in the ready position; parent kneels 10 to 12 feet away with tennis balls.
Parent tosses a short hop that bounces 2 feet in front of the glove.
Child reaches the glove out front, fingers down, and catches the ball just after the bounce with soft hands.
Child flips the ball back and resets; repeat eight times.
Parent tosses long hops that bounce 6 feet out; child stays back and catches them at the top.
Parent tosses in-between hops that bounce 4 feet out; child steps forward to make them short hops.
Parent mixes all three for ten tosses while the child calls 'short' or 'long' before each catch.
Finish with Wall Ball Twenty-One against a garage door with a tennis ball, if a safe wall is available.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove waits back near the body and the short hop jumps up at the chest.
commonMistakes.fix: Lay a glove or towel on the ground 2 feet in front of the toes and have the child catch every hop over that marker.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stabbing at the ball with a stiff arm.
commonMistakes.fix: Toss slowly and ask for a catch so quiet that you cannot hear the ball hit the glove.

commonMistakes.mistake: Freezing in place and taking every ball on the in-between hop.
commonMistakes.fix: Call 'in' or 'back' as you toss until the child starts moving the feet without the call.

commonMistakes.mistake: Lifting the head early on short hops.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask the child to watch the ball touch the ground and then the glove, two separate looks, before lifting the eyes.

cues: Pick your hop with your feet
Reach out and catch it off the ground
Short or long, never in between
See the bounce, see the glove
safety: Tennis balls only for short-hop work at home and for all wall ball; a baseball off a wall or a bad hop at 10 feet is a dental bill.
A tennis ball can still sting an eye at close range, so toss softly, keep the eyes on the ball, and consider sport glasses for players who already wear glasses.
Check the wall for dents and the area for windows and parked cars before any wall ball.

progression.easier: Toss short hops from 6 feet so slowly that the child can watch the bounce and reach without any fear, and skip the wall.
progression.harder: Move to firmer tosses from 15 feet, use a real baseball on a field with a coach rolling, and play Wall Ball Twenty-One for score.
