items.title: Infield Fundamentals: Where to Be on Every Ground Ball
items.objective: The player will be able to name their job on a routine ground ball from any infield position, whether the ball is hit to them or not, and move to that spot without being told.
items.summary: Only one infielder fields each ground ball, but all four infielders, the pitcher, and the catcher have a job on every one. This lesson lays out who covers what so nobody stands and watches.

video.note: The production video will show an animated diamond with six defenders, then a ground ball hit to each infield position in turn, with arrows showing every player's movement to cover a base or back up a throw before cutting to real 11-year-olds doing the same on a field.

explanation: A ground ball to the shortstop is not just the shortstop's play. The first baseman has to get to the bag, the second baseman has to cover second in case a runner is coming, and the pitcher has to move. The catcher has to back up first base in case the throw gets away. When every player knows a job and moves to it, routine ground balls become outs. When they stand still, one bad throw turns into two extra bases.

Start with nobody on base. On a ground ball to the third baseman or the shortstop, the left side of the infield, the throw goes to first. The first baseman gets to the bag, the second baseman moves toward second base to cover it, the pitcher drifts toward the first-base line to back up or help, and the catcher runs down the first-base line in foul territory to back up the throw. The outfielders move too: the right fielder comes in behind first base in case the ball gets past.

On a ground ball to the second baseman, the right side, the shortstop covers second base. On a ground ball to the first baseman, the pitcher sprints to cover first base, because the first baseman may be too far from the bag to get back; the pitcher runs to a spot just inside the first-base line and takes the toss, touching the bag with the right foot while moving toward the infield to avoid the runner. That pitcher-covers-first play is the one most often forgotten by young teams, so teams practice it until it is automatic.

Now put a runner on first base, so the play may go to second for a force out instead of first. On a ground ball to the left side, the second baseman covers second and takes the throw. On a ground ball to the right side, the shortstop covers second. This is the simplest rule of all: the middle infielder who did not field the ball covers the bag. The first baseman still gets to first for a possible second throw, and the third baseman stays home to cover third.

Backing up is as important as covering. Whenever a throw is made, somebody should be lined up behind the receiver in case it sails. The catcher backs up first on throws from the infield, the pitcher backs up third and home on throws from the outfield, and the outfielders back up every throw to a base on their side. Coaches set these responsibilities, and routine coverage can vary a little from team to team, so players should check how their own coach wants it done and then do it every pitch.
parentInstructions: This lesson is mostly thinking, so it can start at the kitchen table. Draw a diamond on paper, place six coins for the pitcher, catcher, and four infielders, and move them around together as you talk through a ground ball to each position.
Ask your child one question at a time: 'Ball is hit to the shortstop. Where do you go if you are the second baseman?' Let them move the coin before you give the answer.
Repeat the pitcher-covers-first play more than any other. It is the one youth teams forget most, and it is the one a parent can quiz in the car.
In the yard, use four bases or shoes to make a small diamond and walk through the coverage at jogging speed with no ball. Call a position and a direction, and your child runs to the correct spot.
Ask your child's coach how the team handles coverage, because some details vary by team, and use the coach's version at home.
Keep sessions to ten minutes and end by letting your child quiz you; explaining it is the fastest way to learn it.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Coins on a hand-drawn diamond at the table, then four shoes in the yard as bases with the child jogging to each coverage spot as you call out where the ball was hit.
steps: Draw a diamond and place six markers for the pitcher, catcher, first, second, shortstop, and third.

Parent calls 'ground ball to the shortstop, nobody on' and the child moves every marker: first baseman to the bag, second baseman to second, pitcher toward the first-base line, catcher down the line behind first.
Parent calls 'ground ball to the first baseman' and the child moves the pitcher to cover first base.
Parent calls 'ground ball to the second baseman' and the child moves the shortstop to cover second.
Parent adds a runner on first and repeats each call; the child decides who covers second for the force.
Move outside to a small diamond made of shoes or bases and repeat the calls with the child running to the right spot.
Add a soft ball: parent rolls to a spot, names the position the child is playing, and the child moves to the correct coverage rather than to the ball.
Finish by having the child teach one coverage back to the parent.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing still and watching when the ball is hit to someone else.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the rule that every player moves on every ball, even if the move is only two steps toward a base.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pitcher forgets to cover first on a ball to the first baseman.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the pitcher say 'ball right side, I go' out loud on every ground ball to the right side in practice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Both middle infielders go to second base or neither does.
commonMistakes.fix: Teach the one rule: the middle infielder who did not field the ball covers second.

commonMistakes.mistake: Catcher stays at home plate on a throw to first with nobody on.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the catcher race the batter down the line in foul ground on every such play at practice until it is a habit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Players learn one team's coverage and argue with a new coach's version.
commonMistakes.fix: Explain that teams differ on details and that the job is to learn and use the current coach's plan.

cues: Ball right side, pitcher covers first
The other middle infielder covers second
Know your job before the pitch
safety: When this is run on a field with live throws, warm up first and use the full infield rotation drill with its throw caps.
The pitcher covering first should touch the inside of the bag and turn into the infield to stay out of the runner's path.
Walk through coverages without a ball before adding one, so nobody is running into a teammate while learning a new spot.

progression.easier: Work only on nobody-on-base coverage, one position at a time, using coins at the table and no ball.
progression.harder: Add runners on first and second, bunt coverage, and live ground balls in the full infield rotation drill at team practice.

items.title: Turning the Double Play: Feeds and Pivots
items.objective: The player will be able to make a chest-high feed to the middle infielder covering second and, as the pivot player, catch the feed, touch the bag, and throw to first in a three-beat rhythm.
items.summary: Two outs on one ground ball is the most satisfying play in the infield. This lesson breaks it into the feed, the pivot, and the throw, and explains who covers second on each side of the diamond.

video.note: The production video will show a 12-year-old shortstop and second baseman turning double plays from both sides in slow motion, with the underhand flip, the overhand feed, and both pivot footwork options labeled on screen.

explanation: A double play happens when there is a runner on first base and fewer than two outs, and a ground ball is turned into two outs: the force at second base, then the throw to first before the batter arrives. It requires three players to do three things quickly and in order. The fielder makes a feed, the middle infielder covering second makes a pivot, and the first baseman catches the final throw. Each piece has its own technique.

Who covers second depends on which side the ball is hit to. On a ball to the shortstop side, which includes balls to the third baseman, the second baseman covers the bag and the shortstop or third baseman feeds. On a ball to the second-base side, which includes balls to the first baseman, the shortstop covers the bag and the second baseman or first baseman feeds. On a ball back to the pitcher, most teams have the shortstop cover, but coaches set this and it can vary by team, so players should confirm the plan at practice.

The feed is a throw to the pivot player's chest, made quickly but under control. When the fielder is close to the bag, say within fifteen feet, the feed is an underhand flip: the fielder turns the glove hand toward the bag, shows the ball so the pivot player can see it the whole way, and pushes it with a stiff wrist and a follow-through toward the chest. When the fielder is farther away, the feed is a short overhand throw after turning the shoulders toward the bag, delivered firm and chest-high with no fancy spin.

The pivot is the job of the player covering second. For the second baseman taking a feed from the shortstop side, one common method is to catch the ball while touching the bag with the left foot, step back off the bag with the right foot toward the outfield, and throw to first from inside the baseline. For the shortstop taking a feed from the second-base side, the usual method is to catch the ball while the right foot drags across the back corner of the bag, continue through, and throw to first. Many coaches teach several versions of each pivot, and players should learn the one their coach prefers before adding others.

Timing is everything. The pivot player must be moving to the bag before the feed is thrown, with both hands up as a target, and should arrive under control rather than at a sprint. Catch, touch, throw should feel like three even beats. Then the pivot player gets out of the runner's path immediately, because a sliding runner is coming into the bag, which is why young players never practice live double plays until the feeds and pivots are reliable without a runner.
parentInstructions: This is a team lesson at heart, but two people can practice the pieces. Stand 15 feet from your child with soft balls and have them practice the underhand flip to your chest: glove hand turned toward you, ball shown the whole way, stiff wrist, follow through to your chest.

Then practice the pivot footwork without a ball. Put a base or a doormat on the ground and have your child jog to it, both hands up, and perform catch-touch-throw in slow motion using the footwork their coach has taught.

Add a ball: toss a feed as your child approaches the bag, and watch for the feet already moving to the base before the ball arrives. A child who waits at the bag standing still is doing it wrong, even if the catch is clean.
Count the beats out loud with your child: 'catch, touch, throw.' The three words should be evenly spaced.
Ask the coach which pivot and which coverage the team uses, and practice only that version at home.
Keep the throws short and soft at home. Full-distance pivot throws to first belong at the field after a warm-up.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A doormat is second base, a sock ball is the feed, and a parent is the target. The flip, the footwork, and the three beats can all be learned in a living room.
steps: Set a base or mat on the ground with a parent 15 feet away as the feeder and a target 30 to 40 feet away as first base.
Child practices ten underhand flips to the parent's chest from 12 feet, showing the ball the whole way.
Child practices ten short overhand feeds from 25 feet, turning the shoulders toward the target before throwing.
Child starts 10 feet from the bag, jogs to it with both hands up, and performs the pivot footwork with no ball, five times slowly.
Parent feeds a soft ball as the child approaches the bag; child catches, touches, and throws to the target in three beats.
Switch sides so the child practices both the second baseman's pivot and the shortstop's pivot.
Child practices the feeder role again, this time with the parent as a moving pivot player.
Finish by having the child explain who covers second on a ball to each infield position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hiding the ball in the glove on the underhand flip so the pivot player cannot see it.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the feeder hold the ball up in the bare hand for a full second before flipping, until showing it becomes a habit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Feeding high or with spin, so the pivot player has to reach.
commonMistakes.fix: Make every feed at home a stiff-wrist push to the chest; a feed that makes the receiver move is a miss.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pivot player arrives at the bag and stops before the feed comes.
commonMistakes.fix: Delay the feed until the player is two steps from the bag so the catch happens on the move.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pivot player throws from on top of the bag and gets tangled with the runner.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice the step off the bag toward the outfield or the drag across the back corner, whichever the coach teaches, until it is automatic.

commonMistakes.mistake: Both middle infielders break to the bag, leaving nobody to field.
commonMistakes.fix: Drill the coverage rule by side of the diamond with coins on a table before taking it to the field.

cues: Show the ball on the flip
safety: Pivot throws to first are full-distance throws; warm up completely and cap the number of them in any session.
No live runners sliding into second until the feeds and pivots are reliable, and never a slide into a fielder's legs.
Hard baseballs only on a field with a first baseman who can handle full throws; use soft balls for all home practice.

progression.easier: Practice only the underhand flip and the no-ball footwork, with no throw to first.
progression.harder: Run the around-the-horn drill at team practice with a stopwatch, add a runner from home in the final round, and learn a second pivot option.

items.title: Outfield Fundamentals: Ground Balls in the Outfield
items.objective: The player will be able to field an outfield ground ball two ways: blocking it with a knee down when no run is at stake, and charging through it to throw when a runner is trying to score.
items.summary: Ground balls that reach the outfield are different from infield grounders. This lesson teaches the safe block that keeps the ball in front and the do-or-die play that gets rid of it fast.

video.note: The production video will show a 10-year-old left fielder fielding ground balls with the knee-down block from the front and side, then the do-or-die charge and throw in slow motion, with a coach calling which play to use.

explanation: When a ground ball gets through the infield, the outfielder's first job is simple: do not let it get past. An infielder who misses a ball gives up a single; an outfielder who misses one gives up two or three bases. Because of that, outfielders field ground balls differently depending on how much is at stake.

The safe play is the block. With no runner trying to score, the outfielder gets in front of the ball, drops the throwing-side knee to the ground, and makes a wall with the body. The glove goes down between the legs with the fingers pointing at the grass, the bare hand covers on top, and the glove-side leg stays bent with the foot flat so the fielder can pop up quickly. If the ball takes a bad hop, it hits the body and stays in front, which is the whole point.

The aggressive play is called do-or-die. With a runner rounding third and the game on the line, there is no time to block. The outfielder charges the ball under control, fields it outside the glove-side foot while moving forward, and throws in the same motion. It looks like the infield slow-roller play but with a longer throw. If the ball takes a bad hop on a do-or-die, it may get past, which is why this play is saved for the moments that demand it.

Both plays end with a throw to the cutoff man, the infielder who comes out to meet the ball. After the block, the outfielder stands up, takes a crow hop toward the target, and throws chest-high so the cutoff can catch it and redirect it. After a do-or-die, the throw goes right away, still aimed at the cutoff's chest, because a throw that sails over the cutoff cannot be redirected to a different base.

Deciding which play to use is part of the skill. Before every pitch the outfielder should know how many outs there are, where the runners are, and how fast they are. A fielder who has decided in advance does not have to think when the ball is hit; the knee goes down or the feet charge, and the play is already half made.
parentInstructions: You need grass and room: a park or field with 90 feet to spare. Stand 60 feet from your child with soft balls or tennis balls, and set a target 60 feet to the side where the cutoff would stand.
Call the play before each roll. 'Block it!' means knee down and a wall; 'Do or die!' means charge and throw in one motion.
On the block, watch which knee drops. For a right-handed thrower it is the right knee, so the left leg stays bent and ready to push up into the throw.
On do-or-die, watch the last steps; the ball should be fielded outside the glove-side foot while the body keeps moving forward.
Have every throw go to the target, not back to you, and ask for chest-high throws the target can catch without moving.
Ten throws is a full session for an outfield lesson. These are long throws and should follow an easy warm-up.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Roll a tennis ball across a lawn and have the child block it knee-down or charge it do-or-die, then jog it back to you. The decision and the body position are the lesson.
steps: Child starts 60 feet from the parent; a target waits 60 feet to the side as the cutoff.
Parent calls 'Block it!' and rolls a ground ball at the child.
Child gets in front, drops the throwing-side knee, puts the glove down between the legs with the bare hand covering, and fields the ball.
Child stands, crow hops toward the target, and throws chest-high to the cutoff.
Parent calls 'Do or die!' and rolls another ball.
Child charges under control, fields outside the glove-side foot while moving, and throws to the cutoff in one motion.
Alternate calls for ten balls, then mix them without a pattern.
Finish by asking the child which play they would choose with a runner on second and two outs, and why.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the wrong knee so the throw is slow and awkward.
commonMistakes.fix: Put a towel on the ground where the throwing-side knee should land and have the child kneel on it before every block.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fielding the ball to the side instead of in front of the body on the block.
commonMistakes.fix: Roll softly and insist the child's belt buckle faces the ball before the knee drops.

commonMistakes.mistake: Charging a ball when the block was the right play.
commonMistakes.fix: Call the situation out loud before each roll and praise the correct decision over the result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Standing up and throwing from flat feet after the block.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice the stand-and-crow-hop ten times with no ball until it is one motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing over the cutoff's head.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the cutoff hold both hands up and require every throw to be caught without a jump.

cues: Hit the cutoff in the chest
safety: Outfield throws are the longest in the game; warm up first and keep the session to about ten throws.
Hard baseballs only on a mowed field; use tennis balls or soft balls on a bumpy park lawn.
Walk the grass for holes and sprinkler heads before any charging play.

progression.easier: Practice only the knee-down block with slow rolls and no throw, until the body shape is automatic.
progression.harder: Add a parent running from third to home on each roll so the child has to choose the play and beat the runner to the cutoff.

items.title: Outfield: Hitting the Cutoff Man
items.objective: The player will be able to throw from the outfield to the cutoff man's chest, and as the cutoff man, line up between the ball and the base and relay the throw in one motion.
items.summary: A long throw that sails over everyone's head is the most common way youth teams give away extra bases. This lesson teaches outfielders to hit the cutoff and teaches the cutoff to catch and relay cleanly.

video.note: The production video will show a ball hit to the right-field gap with the shortstop sprinting out as the cutoff, hands up, the outfielder throwing to his chest, and the relay throw home, filmed from an elevated angle so the straight line from ball to cutoff to base is clear.

explanation: The cutoff man is the infielder who runs out between the outfielder and the base where the play is, to catch the outfielder's throw and send it the rest of the way. Young outfielders often believe the heroic play is to throw all the way home on one bounce. In reality a throw to the cutoff is faster, more accurate, and gives the defense a choice, because the cutoff can throw to any base or hold the ball if there is no play.

Which infielder goes out depends on where the ball is hit. On a ball to left field or left-center, the shortstop usually goes out as the cutoff. On a ball to right field or right-center, the second baseman usually goes. On throws coming home, the first baseman or third baseman often becomes the cutoff in front of the plate. Coaches organize these assignments for their own teams, and they can vary, so players should learn their team's system and run it every time.

The cutoff's job is to make a straight line. The cutoff sprints out, turns to face the outfielder, and lines up exactly between the ball and the base where the throw will go, usually 40 to 60 feet from the outfielder for younger players. Both hands go up over the head as a big target, and the body stands sideways so the glove-side shoulder points at the outfielder. Standing square with the glove at the hip is slow and gives the outfielder a small target.

The outfielder's job is to hit that target. After fielding the ball, the outfielder crow hops toward the cutoff and throws chest-high, hard enough to get there quickly but never so high that it sails over the cutoff's head. A one-hop throw to the cutoff is better than a throw the cutoff cannot reach. The outfielder is aiming at the cutoff's chest, not at the base beyond.

Then the relay. The cutoff catches on the glove-side shoulder, turns toward the glove side so the throw can continue without a stop, and throws to the base in one motion, or holds the ball if the players behind are yelling to cut and hold. Infielders behind the cutoff call 'cut two' or 'cut home' or 'cut, cut' to tell the cutoff where the ball should go, which is why the cutoff keeps the ears open and never turns around to look.
parentInstructions: You need three people for the full picture, but two can practice. Stand 50 feet from your child with your hands up over your head as the cutoff and have your child crow hop and throw to your chest from a rolled ground ball.
Then switch: you roll or throw the ball to a spot 50 feet away, your child sprints out as the cutoff, turns, lines up between the ball and a base marked by a shoe, and puts both hands up.
Watch the body. The cutoff should stand sideways with the glove-side shoulder pointing at the ball, not square with the glove at the hip.
Throw the ball to your child's chest and watch the relay: catch on the glove-side shoulder, turn toward the glove side, throw to the shoe in one motion.
Yell 'cut!' on some throws so your child practices catching and holding instead of relaying. The ears are part of this lesson.
These are long throws for a child. Warm up first and stop at about 10 throws per role.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Use a tennis ball and shoes as bases. The outfielder throws a tennis ball to a parent cutoff with hands up, and the parent relays it softly to a shoe; the lining-up and the one-motion turn are the skills.
steps: Place a shoe as the target base and stand 50 feet from your child as the cutoff with both hands up.
Roll a ground ball to your child, who fields it, crow hops toward you, and throws chest-high to your hands.
Repeat five times, then switch roles: you become the outfielder and your child becomes the cutoff.
Roll the ball 50 feet away from the shoe; your child sprints out, turns, and lines up between the ball and the shoe with both hands up and the body sideways.
Throw the ball to the child's chest; the child catches on the glove-side shoulder, turns to the glove side, and throws to the shoe in one motion.
Add a voice: yell 'relay!' or 'cut!' as the ball is in the air so the child decides to throw or hold.
Repeat five relays, then finish with the child explaining who the cutoff is on a ball to left field and a ball to right field.

commonMistakes.mistake: Outfielder throws over the cutoff's head toward the base.
commonMistakes.fix: Make the rule that any throw the cutoff cannot catch with the feet on the ground counts as an error, even if it reaches the base.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutoff stands square to the outfielder with the glove at the hip.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the cutoff hold both hands over the head and turn sideways before the outfielder is allowed to throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutoff lines up off to one side instead of between the ball and the base.
commonMistakes.fix: Stretch a string or lay a line of cones from the outfielder to the base and have the cutoff stand on it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cutoff catches, stops, and then looks for the base.
commonMistakes.fix: Practice the catch-and-turn with a parent calling the base before the ball arrives, so the cutoff knows where it goes.

cues: Hit the cutoff in the chest
Hands up, be a big target
Line up between the ball and the base
Catch on the glove side, turn to the glove side
safety: Long throws require a full warm-up; this should be the last throwing lesson of a session and should stop at about 10 throws per role.
Hard baseballs only on a field with players who can catch full-effort throws; otherwise soft or tennis balls.
Keep the relay line clear of other players, and never run a second line close enough that a wild throw could reach it.

progression.easier: Shorten both throws to 30 feet with a tennis ball and practice only the hands-up lineup and the one-motion turn.
progression.harder: Run the cutoff relay race at team practice, add live runners, and have infielders call 'cut two' or 'cut home' for the cutoff to react to.

items.title: Soft Hands: Catching With Two Hands
items.objective: The player will be able to catch a softly tossed ball with the glove and the bare hand working together, giving slightly toward the body so the ball stays in the glove.
items.summary: Young players who catch with the glove alone drop half of what they touch. This lesson teaches the alligator catch and the soft give that keeps the ball in the pocket.

video.note: The production video will show close-ups of a 6-year-old's glove and bare hand coming together on soft tosses, with a slow-motion comparison of a stiff one-handed stab that pops out and a relaxed two-handed catch that stays in.

explanation: A glove does not catch a ball by itself, especially a stiff new glove on a small hand. The ball lands in the pocket and bounces right back out unless something stops it. That something is the bare hand. Teaching children to catch with two hands is the fastest way to turn drops into catches, and it also puts the ball in the throwing hand sooner for the throw that comes next.

The picture that works for young children is an alligator. The glove is the bottom jaw, held open with the pocket facing the ball. The bare hand is the top jaw, hovering just above the glove with the fingers spread. When the ball lands in the bottom jaw, the top jaw chomps down on it, and the alligator pulls its meal to its belly. Children remember the alligator long after they forget the words.

Soft hands is the other half. If the arms are stiff and the glove is jammed forward at the ball, the ball hits a hard surface and pops out. If the arms are relaxed and the hands give back a few inches toward the body as the ball arrives, the glove absorbs the ball like a pillow. Parents can hear the difference: a loud smack is stiff hands, a quiet thud is soft hands.

Where the hands meet the ball depends on height. For a ball at the belly or below, the glove fingers point down and the bare hand covers from above. For a ball at the chest or higher, the glove fingers point up and the bare hand comes in from the side, thumbs close together. The alligator still chomps; it just tilts its head.

Children in this age group should learn all of this with a soft safety ball tossed underhand from close range. Speed and distance add nothing until the two-handed catch is automatic. The goal of a session is not how many catches were made but how many were made with both hands.
parentInstructions: Kneel 6 to 8 feet from your child with a soft safety ball. Kneeling keeps your tosses gentle and your eyes level with the glove.
Make the alligator together before the first toss: glove open as the bottom jaw, bare hand open above as the top jaw, and chomp three times while saying the word.
Toss underhand to the belly, slow and easy. Watch the top jaw: it should close over the ball the moment it lands, and both hands should pull in to the belly.
Listen to the catch. A loud smack means stiff arms; say 'soft hands' and toss even slower until the sound gets quiet.
After ten belly tosses, send a few to the knees and a few to the chest so the alligator learns to tilt its head.
Ask your child to flip the ball back underhand. Twenty tosses is plenty; stop while they are still asking for more.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: A sock ball and two bare hands make a perfect alligator: one hand is the bottom jaw, the other is the top jaw, and the chomp in the middle is the catch.
steps: Child puts on a glove and makes the alligator: glove open below, bare hand open above.
Parent kneels 6 to 8 feet away and tosses a soft ball underhand to the child's belly.
Glove catches, bare hand chomps down on top, and both hands pull the ball to the belly.
Child says 'got it' and flips the ball back underhand.
Repeat ten belly-high tosses, listening for quiet catches.
Parent tosses five balls to the knees; alligator points its nose at the ground.
Parent tosses five balls to the chest; alligator points its nose at the sky.
Finish with three tosses where the parent says nothing and watches whether the top jaw shows up on its own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Bare hand hangs at the side and the ball pops out of the glove.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child hold the bare hand above the glove before each toss and keep it there until the chomp.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stabbing at the ball with a locked elbow.
commonMistakes.fix: Ask for a catch so quiet you cannot hear it, and toss slower until it happens.

commonMistakes.mistake: Snapping the glove shut before the ball arrives.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child count 'one' when the ball touches the glove and chomp on 'two' for a few tosses, then let it blend.

commonMistakes.mistake: Glove held flat like a plate so the ball rolls off.
commonMistakes.fix: Tilt the glove so the pocket faces the parent and check that the parent can see the whole pocket before tossing.

cues: Top jaw covers, bottom jaw catches
safety: Soft safety balls only for ages 4-8, even when the child begs for a real one.
Keep tosses below the shoulders at this age so nothing drifts toward the face.
Check that the glove is small enough to close; a glove that is too big teaches one-handed trapping.

progression.easier: Toss a sock ball to two bare hands from 4 feet, and let the catch be a hug against the chest.
progression.harder: Back up to 15 feet, add gentle tosses to each side so the feet move before the alligator chomps, and begin a quick transfer to the throwing hand.

items.title: Afraid of the Ball? Building Confidence With Soft Balls
items.objective: The player will be able to keep the eyes open and the hands ready as a ball comes toward them, moving at their own pace from a rolled sock ball to a tossed soft safety ball.
items.summary: Fear of the ball is normal, common, and fixable. This lesson gives parents a step-by-step progression from a sock ball to a tennis ball to a soft safety baseball, with the parent's job spelled out at every stage.

video.note: The production video will follow one 5-year-old across four short sessions, from flinching at a rolled sock ball to catching an underhand toss of a soft safety ball with open eyes, with the parent narrating what they did at each step.

explanation: Being afraid of a ball coming at you is not a flaw. It is the brain doing its job, because something flying toward the face is exactly what the brain is built to avoid. Almost every child feels this at some point, and many adults still flinch at a hard ball. The fear usually shows up as a head that turns away, eyes that close, hands that pull back, or a child who suddenly wants to do anything but catch. None of those are signs of a child who cannot play baseball; they are signs of a child who has not yet learned that this particular ball will not hurt.

The way through is to prove it with the body, not with words, one small step at a time. Stage one is a rolled sock ball, which cannot hurt anyone and never comes near the face, so the child can practice watching a moving object arrive with the eyes open. The parent sits on the floor, rolls slowly, and says nothing about fear at all. The only thing to praise is open eyes. When ten rolls in a row are scooped with the eyes open, the child, not the parent, decides whether to try a gentle underhand toss of the sock ball to the belly.

Stage two is a tennis ball. It is firmer and bounces, which is a bigger change than it sounds. Go back to the beginning: roll it first, then toss it to the belly. Let the child squeeze it, bounce it, and even bump it against a leg on purpose to prove it is harmless. The parent's job in this stage is to keep the tosses low and slow, to toss from the front so the child can always see the ball, and to drop back to rolling without a word of disappointment if the head starts turning away.

Stage three is a soft safety baseball, the squishy kind used in tee ball, and because it looks like a real baseball it can bring the fear back for a day. Start over again with rolls, then belly-high tosses from 6 feet, then slightly higher tosses once the eyes stay open. Add the glove when the child wants it, with the bare hand on top. The parent's job here is patience: a stage might take one session or three weeks, and both are normal. Real hard baseballs are not part of this progression at all; they can wait until the child is older and asking for one.

A few rules hold at every stage. Never sneak in a harder ball or a faster toss to see what happens, because one surprise sting can erase weeks of trust. Never tease, compare the child to a sibling, or say 'it won't hurt' while the child is scared, since the child cannot believe it yet. End every session with a few catches the child is certain to make, so the last feeling of the day is success. And let the child hold the controls: a child who chooses when to move up will move up faster than a child who is pushed.
parentInstructions: Start on the floor with a rolled-up pair of socks, 6 feet apart. Say this is a game about being brave, that being scared is normal, and that nobody is ever in trouble for being scared.
Roll slowly along the floor and praise only one thing out loud: open eyes. Say 'I saw you watch it all the way in.' Do not mention the fear again during the session.
Move to the next ball only when your child chooses to, and never the same day a harder ball was first introduced. Keep the tennis ball and the soft safety ball out of sight until then.
With each new ball, go back to rolling before any toss, then toss underhand from the front to the belly, low and slow, so your child can see the whole flight.
If the head turns away or the eyes close, drop back one step without comment and try again next time. Dropping back is part of the plan, not a failure.
Finish every session with five catches your child is sure to make, then stop, even if it is going well. Wanting more is the best possible ending.
Keep all real baseballs put away during this period, including for your own catches with others, so your child never hears a hard ball smack a glove nearby.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: The first stage uses nothing but a rolled pair of socks, and a child can stay there as long as they need. A tennis ball and a soft safety ball join later, when the child chooses.
steps: Sit on the floor 6 feet from the child with a sock ball and explain the brave game and the one rule: the child picks when to move up.
Roll the sock ball slowly ten times; praise open eyes after every roll, and say nothing else about the catching.
When the child chooses, toss the sock ball underhand to the belly from 6 feet, ten times, with the child squeezing it and saying 'soft' after each catch.
Bring out the tennis ball and start over with ten slow rolls, then ten belly tosses. Let the child bump it against a leg on purpose to feel that it does not hurt.
Bring out the soft safety baseball and start over again: ten rolls, then ten belly tosses from 6 feet, then tosses to the chest once the eyes stay open.
Add the glove when the child asks for it, with the bare hand covering, and keep tosses at the belly for the first glove session.
At any sign of the head turning or the eyes closing, drop back one step for the rest of that day without comment.
End every session with five sure catches and a high five, and let the child color one rung on a brave ladder chart for each step they chose to climb.

commonMistakes.mistake: Head turns away or eyes close as the ball arrives.
commonMistakes.fix: Lower the toss or go back to rolling, and ask the child to call out the color of the ball as it reaches their hands.

commonMistakes.mistake: Parent speeds up or switches balls to test whether the child is really still scared.
commonMistakes.fix: Let the child own every step up; a surprise sting costs weeks and a slow week costs nothing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hands pull back toward the body before the ball arrives.
commonMistakes.fix: Have the child hold a target position with the hands out front and make the ball come to the hands so they never have to reach.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing the child to a sibling or teammate who is not afraid.
commonMistakes.fix: Talk only about this child's own ladder and how many rungs they have climbed since last week.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pushing through tears to finish the planned number of tosses.
commonMistakes.fix: Stop, roll three easy ones the child cannot miss, celebrate those, and end the session early.

cues: You pick when we move up
Watch it all the way in
safety: Sock balls, tennis balls, and soft safety balls only; hard baseballs are never part of this lesson at any stage.
Toss from the front, underhand, low and slow, so the child always sees the ball coming and nothing drifts toward the face.
Keep sessions short and stop at the first tears; a scared child who is pushed learns to avoid the glove, not the fear.

progression.easier: Stay with the rolled sock ball for as many sessions as needed, and let the child roll it to the parent half the time so the ball is coming and going equally.
progression.harder: Once the soft safety ball is caught at the chest with open eyes, move to the Ready Position lesson and the two-hands lesson, keeping the soft ball for several more weeks.
